transcript: Here are three ads we're trailing this week at my agency may. No. 1 is the flow chart funnel. This format acts really well because it hijacks the brain's pattern sinking instinct. The viewer self diagnoses themselves by finding the symptoms through the branches. Suddenly the ad fields personal instead of random. And because every path leads to the same product, it lands as the answer they arrived at themselves rather than one that they were sold to. No. 2 is the feature call out. Okay, Maddie, this isn't an original ad at all, but this format works well because it gives the brain a reason to justify what the eye already wants. The aesthetic makes you stop and desire the look, but desire alone feels impulsive so people hesitate. The feature callouts high rise pockets, pocket the tuck details hand you the logic to back the feeling. Now it's not I want it, but it's actually like this is a practical piece. And in fashion where most brands sell the fantasy and skip the function, spelling out the practicality really does feel refreshing, which builds trust while everyone else is just doing fit checks and posing. Add format No. 3 is the time stamp. So this format works really well because it answers the question, stopping the sale before the buyer even ask it. Will I actually wear this? Will I actually get a good cost per wear? With Desire first products, people don't doubt that they want it. They want it. They doubt that they'll get their money. Worth time stamps across different scenarios. Do the maths for them. One piece, five outfits, one morning tonight. So every new scene lowers the cost per wear in the consumer's head. So by the end, it doesn't feel like a splurge. It feels like a smart buy. Comment below and guess which ad will work best.
